t.7.44.1: When they had all sat down, downcast in spirit, Kākutstha spoke these words to them, his face withered and parched.
t.7.44.2: Listen, all of you, may good fortune be yours, and do not let your minds turn otherwise: hear what kind of talk is going on among the citizens about me and Sītā.
t.7.44.3: A very great and loathsome slander against me is current among the townsfolk and likewise among the people of the countryside; it cuts me to the very quick.
t.7.44.4: I, indeed, was born in the family of the great-souled Ikṣvākus; how could I bring Sītā, whose conduct is sinful, into the city?
t.7.44.5: For you know, gentle one, how Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa in the lonely forest of Daṇḍaka, and how he was destroyed by me.
t.7.44.6: Before your very eyes, O Saumitri, the bearer of the gods' oblations, Agni, declared Maithilī sinless, and so did Vāyu, who moves through the sky.
t.7.44.7: And formerly, in the presence of the gods and of all the ṛṣis, the Moon and the Sun declared the daughter of Janaka to be sinless.
t.7.44.8: Thus she, pure in conduct, was placed in my hand by the great Indra on the island of Laṅkā, in the presence of the gods and Gandharvas.
t.7.44.9: My inmost self, too, knows Sītā, the illustrious one, to be pure; therefore, taking Vaidehī with me, I came to Ayodhyā.
t.7.44.10: But this great talk and grief dwell in my heart: the very great censure of the citizens, and likewise of the people of the countryside.
t.7.44.11: Any being whose infamy is sung in the world falls indeed to the lowest worlds, and remains there for as long as that report is spoken of.
t.7.44.12: Infamy is condemned by the gods, while fame is honored among the gods; indeed, every undertaking of the great-souled is for the sake of fame.
t.7.44.14: Therefore, behold me, sirs, fallen into an ocean of grief; for I see no sorrow at all greater than this.
t.7.44.13: Fearful of public reproach, I would give up even my life, or even you, O bulls among men; how much more, then, the daughter of Janaka!
t.7.44.15: Tomorrow at daybreak, O Saumitri, mount the chariot driven by Sumantra, place Sītā upon it, and leave her at the border of the realm.
t.7.44.16: On the far bank of the Gaṅgā lies the hermitage of the great-souled Vālmīki, heavenly in appearance, resting upon the bank of the Tamasā.
t.7.44.17: Leave her there in a lonely thicket, O Raghunandana, and come back quickly, O Saumitri; do as I say.
t.7.44.18: I am not to be answered back in any way concerning Sītā, for if I were opposed in this, it would cause me the greatest displeasure.
t.7.44.19: And I adjure you all by my two arms and by my life, you who would in any way speak to me in the midst of my words to try to win me over.
t.7.44.20: If you abide by my command, honor me, sirs: let Sītā be taken away from here today; do as I say.
t.7.44.21: Earlier I was told by her, "I would like to see the great hermitages on the bank of the Gaṅgā"; so let this wish of hers be fulfilled.
t.7.44.22: Having spoken thus, Kākutstha, his eyes veiled with tears, that righteous-souled one, surrounded by his brothers, entered within.
